speaker: Pieter van der Does
title: Adyen success story: Pieter van der Does building one of Europe’s largest fintech unicorns
question: In venture-backed startups, why can granting liquidation preferences to new investors create dangerous misalignment when a company hits a rough patch?
guest: We wanted the relationship with our investors to be very simple, and simple to my belief is that if the current shareholders gain, the new shareholders gain; if the current lose, the new shareholders lose. In practice, in an investment round, new investors often get liquidation preferences. What I've seen is that if the company hits a rough patch, the liquidation preference can mean that a shareholder says, 'Even if we get a low offer, let's just sell it—I'll get my money back, I get my minimum return, that's fantastic.' And that's really bad for the entrepreneurs and the other shareholders. So we said there is always risk and return: we make the risk a little higher for the investor by having everyone take common shares with no preference for anyone, and then it's up to the investor to price that risk into the valuation. You could claim you could have raised at a higher valuation by giving away more rights, but keeping everyone's interests aligned around the table is what keeps the company moving forward cleanly.

points.core: Liquidation preferences break symmetric outcomes across a company's shareholder base.
points.note: Accept: preferred stock destroys the rule that all shareholders win together or lose together, creating asymmetric payoffs. Do not credit: merely defining what a liquidation preference is.

points.core: Downside protection lets preferred investors recover minimum returns from lowball offers.
points.note: Accept: in a mediocre or low acquisition offer, preferred holders still get their money back or guaranteed return first. Do not credit: vague statements that preferred investors get paid first without connecting to low offers.

points.core: Preferred holders face incentives to force premature sales that harm common shareholders.
points.note: Accept: during a rough patch, protected investors push to sell the company cheaply at the expense of founders and earlier shareholders. Do not credit: generic claims that VCs are short-termist.

points.core: Issuing only common stock shifts risk into valuation instead of divergent rights.
points.note: Accept: refusing preferences may mean accepting a lower headline valuation so investors price the extra risk upfront while keeping incentives unified. Do not credit: claiming founders can always get both top valuation and zero preferences.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Liquidation preferences give investors the right to get their money back (sometimes a multiple of it) before common shareholders see anything. In good times this barely matters, because a large exit leaves plenty for everyone. In a rough patch, though, the stacked preferences can exceed or approach the company's realistic exit value, and that splits the cap table into groups with conflicting incentives.

Founders and employees, who hold common stock, may find their equity effectively worthless in any modest sale. They lose motivation to stay, or they favor long-shot gambles, since only a huge outcome pays them anything. Preferred investors face the opposite pull: because they are paid first, they may push for a quick, low-priced sale or liquidation that returns their capital, even if patience would create more total value.

Layers of preferences also pit investors against each other. Senior late-stage holders may accept an exit that wipes out junior early-stage holders, complicating board votes, new financing and acquisition negotiations.

The result is a company whose key decision-makers no longer benefit from the same outcome at exactly the moment it most needs unified effort. This is why distressed deals often require management carve-outs or recapitalizations.

points.why: The response explains how preferences can let one group recover value from the same exit that wipes out another.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer: Granting liquidation preferences—especially senior or multiple-return terms—creates a preference stack that pays new investors first in a sale or wind-down, pushing founders, employees, and earlier backers further back in line. When a startup hits a rough patch and its valuation falls near or below this preference overhang, incentives fracture across the cap table. New investors protected by senior preferences may favor a quick, modest acquisition that safely recovers their capital, even if that price wipes out junior preferred and common shareholders completely. Conversely, founders and early investors whose equity sits underwater gain nothing from a moderate sale, incentivizing them to reject reasonable offers and gamble on high-risk turnarounds just to clear the stack. Meanwhile, key employees who realize their options are worthless beneath heavy preferences often lose motivation or depart right when execution matters most. Resulting boardroom battles over blocking rights, dilutive recapitalizations, and management carve-outs can paralyze decision-making and scare off future backers, turning a survivable downturn into a value-destroying stalemate.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Liquidation preferences guarantee that preferred investors get their money back, often 1x and sometimes more, plus any participation rights, before common holders (founders and employees) see anything in a sale. When the company is doing well, this hardly matters, because everyone gets paid. When the company struggles and the likely exit value falls near or below the total preference stack, incentives split apart.

Common holders may expect nothing from a modest acquisition. Their stake behaves like an out-of-the-money option, so they may push for risky, long-shot strategies, or lose motivation and leave. Preferred holders, especially those who invested late at high valuations, may want a quick, safe sale that returns their capital, even if it wipes out everyone else. The board, often controlled by investors, then faces conflicts over sales, recapitalizations, and new down rounds. Delaware cases like *Trados* show this can create fiduciary-duty litigation.

Each new round usually adds preferences on top of earlier ones, so the stack keeps growing. In a rough patch, this can leave the people running the company with little reason to save it, and the people funding it with good reason to sell it cheaply.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer: Liquidation preferences guarantee that new investors get paid back their investment—sometimes at a multiple—before common shareholders like founders and employees receive anything in an exit. When a startup hits a rough patch and its realistic sale value falls near or below that preference stack, incentives fracture sharply. In a modest acquisition, preferred investors might recover their capital or even turn a profit, while founders and employees walk away with nothing. As a result, senior investors often favor a safe, early sale to protect their downside, whereas founders and junior stakeholders have nothing to lose and are incentivized to take extreme, high-risk bets in hopes of clearing the preference overhang. Worse still, senior preferences granted during a down round can push earlier investors and employee equity completely underwater, destroying morale, driving away key talent, and paralyzing board decisions just when unified execution matters most.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Liquidation preferences let investors get paid before founders and employees who hold common stock when a company is sold. In a rough patch, the likely sale price can fall close to the amount owed to preferred investors. A sale might then return most or all of a new investor’s money while leaving the people running the company with little or nothing.

That changes what each side has to lose. The investor may favor an early sale to protect its recovery, while founders and employees may favor a risky turnaround because their shares only pay off if the company’s value rises above the preference. If employees see little chance of their equity paying out, they may leave just when the company needs them most. The misalignment is sharper when new investors get priority over earlier investors or negotiate the right to recover more than they invested.
